                        IntroductionRainfall from the West African monsoon (WAM) is the cornerstone of food security and the economy for hundreds of millions of people1,2. The WAM affords more than 80% of the total annual rainfall necessary for food production and livelihoods. Disentangling plausible pathways of WAM rainfall projections is therefore crucial for supporting climate services that inform sustainable adaptation strategies. The region, however, remains one of the greatest challenges for global climate modelling. Climate models’ development has advanced dramatically, but global projections of the WAM are still fraught with persistent divergences within the models3,4.The advent of the sixth phase of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP65) has brought improvements in resolution and process complexity. Nevertheless, precipitation projections for West Africa throughout the 21st century still show considerable spread, ranging from significant increases in wetness to severe drying6,7. The lack of consensus among models is largely attributed to systematic biases in the simulation of large-scale atmospheric dynamics, particularly the pressure gradient between the Sahara and the South Atlantic Ocean, as well as the representation of low-level moisture fluxes8,9. The canonical practice of using the ensemble mean (EnsMean) is increasingly criticized because it treats models with radically different physical performances equally10,11,12.The question of what plausible trajectories WAM precipitation will follow remains timely. Assessment approaches based on physical processes and mechanisms underpinning the monsoon system have been suggested to replace the former simple quantification of performance against observations13. This is because performance-based evaluation does not guarantee that the model plausibly reproduces the observed climatology, i.e., that the processes underlying simulated climatology are those behind observed ones. Furthermore, it is difficult to derive performance metrics to constrain future projections, since historical accuracy does not guarantee future reliability. This highlights the need for emergent constraints, which link observable variations in the contemporary climate to the long-term sensitivity of the climate system11,14. The process-oriented evaluation approaches consist of giving more credence to models that are able to simulate plausible processes associated with projected patterns. A plausible process can be identified in observations/reanalyses or is likely to occur, i.e. physically explainable, under global warming. This approach is also limited because it cannot go beyond the most state-of-the-art knowledge we have of the functioning of the climate system. The advent of artificial intelligence (AI) in climate science offers an opportunity to overcome this limitation. Indeed, deep learning, and more specifically artificial neural networks (ANNs), offer an unprecedented ability to extract complex spatial features, linear and non-linear relationships within large climate datasets15,16,17. Unlike traditional linear regression methods, ANNs excel at mapping interconnected and multi-dimensional teleconnection patterns, such as multi-pole sea surface temperature (SST) or pressure anomalies15, to local/regional variables, thereby reducing reliance on performance metrics derived solely from raw model outputs and the systematic biases associated with them.In this study, we propose a physical fidelity weighting approach combining deep learning with climate projections and reanalyses. This approach utilizes the Sahelian monsoon ocean-pressure index (SMOPI; see the “Methods” section), as a key spatiotemporal tracer of WAM rainfall18. We train ANNs to learn the dynamic relationship between the spatiotemporal structures of sea level pressure boxes of the SMOPI and monsoon precipitation. Using the Japanese 55-year reanalysis (JRA-5519) as a ground truth reference to force these pre-trained models, we quantify the degree of physical realism of the 11 CMIP6 models (see Supplementary Table 1). Raw projections are thus converted into an ANN-forced weighted ensemble where each model contributes proportionally to its demonstrated ability to reproduce observed teleconnections. Our results show that this approach reduces the inter-model spread by up to 30%. It also corrects the cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) of precipitation, making the distribution closer to historical observations, thereby increasing the plausibility of projections, as demonstrated by the pseudo-observation method (see the subsection “The pseudo-observation approach” in the “Methods” section). Furthermore, models with physically consistent teleconnections project clearer emerging shifts in precipitation distributions because they more accurately translate large-scale oceanic and dynamical signals into regional rainfall responses. By validating our approach on independent members (inter-member transfer learning from Member 1 to Member 2; see the subsection “ANNs: model architecture and training protocol” in the “Methods” section), we demonstrate the temporal stability of this learned physical relationship. This work offers a new way to constrain regional climate projections, thus providing a more robust scientific basis for resilience policies in West Africa.ResultsANNs capture how WAM precipitation responds to SMOPI SLP boxesThe first step involves informing the ANNs of the physics underlying the WAM precipitation. This is a complex task because the forcing factors of the WAM system operate across multiple scales, from local processes to global phenomena20. Furthermore, these factors act on timescales ranging from synoptic events to multi-decadal cycles. The WAM system is more than just a reversal of the ocean-continent thermal and pressure contrasts, often simplified as a large-scale sea breeze, that transports oceanic moisture inland. It is also an integral part of the energetic reorganization of tropical overturning circulations, including the Walker and Hadley cells, and the intertropical convergence zone (ITCZ)21. Consequently, the WAM is influenced by large-scale teleconnections originating from the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific Oceans. The choice of the predictor is therefore critical, as it must account for the WAM’s specific complexity while remaining as simple as possible so that the ANN model can learn both linear and non-linear drivers of the WAM precipitation without overfitting. The Sahel monsoon ocean-pressure index (SMOPI) appears to be the most appropriate in this context (see the subsection “SMOPI” in the “Methods” section). The effectiveness of monsoon monitoring relies on the indicator’s ability to integrate multidimensional processes. It is demonstrated that the SMOPI captures not only regional drivers in the Sahel but also global teleconnections, while remaining effective across sub-seasonal to multi-decadal timescales18. These include, among others, the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO22), the Atlantic Meridional Mode (AMM23), and the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD24), to name a few. In addition, the SMOPI explains the dominant mode of interannual variability in Sahelian rainfall (PC1, up to 74.4% of total variance), exhibiting strong interannual correlations (up to r = 0.75 in reanalyses)18. A remarkable result emerges when the analysis is extended to the entire West African region: the identified sea-level pressure (SLP) boxes remain almost identical and consistent (Supplementary Fig. 1), which is not surprising, as the Sahel monsoonal rainfall is just a regional expression of a larger WAM system20,25. This indicates that SMOPI can also be extended at the scale of the whole WAM system. Therefore, we used the five SMOPI’s SLP boxes (Supplementary Fig. 1) as input predictors, with the June–July–August–September (JJAS) monsoon precipitation being the predictand. The physically-derived SLP boxes are provided to the ANN without imposing the SMOPI formulation18, thereby allowing the ANN to learn its own dynamical relationship between circulation and rainfall. An attribution analysis based on Shapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) revealed that within the SMOPI signal, regional drivers heavily dominate the direct circulation-rainfall coupling over remote basins (Mouassom et al., under review). Specifically, the local Sahel landmass (Box 1, 54.63%) and the northern tropical Atlantic (Box 5, 32.55%) explain the vast majority of the model’s physical importance. Indeed, Box 1 (Supplementary Fig. 1) directly samples the core of the monsoon engine, where surface pressure variability reflects the intensity of the Saharan heat low (SHL) and low-level moisture convergence26. This strong local coupling is consistent with the established role of the SHL as a key driver regulating the WAM onset and intensity27. Meanwhile, Box 5 regulates the thermodynamic boundary governing low-level oceanic moisture advection, anchoring the critical SST gradients that feed moisture into the Sahelian interior28. Conversely, the footprints of remote oceanic basins from the southern Atlantic (Box 2, 8.46%), the tropical Pacific/ENSO (Box 4, 3.09%), and the southern Indian Ocean (Box 3, 1.27%) exhibit much smaller direct surface pressure weights. This lower direct weight aligns with the understanding that their physical influence on the monsoon acts mainly through indirect upper-tropospheric wave propagation and teleconnected regional subsidence rather than localized surface pressure gradients, as widely documented for ENSO29 and Mediterranean/Indian Ocean remote forcings30. The idea is to use the trained ANN model to project plausible future changes in the WAM precipitation under SSP5-8.5 warming scenarios. Given the importance of spatial variability within these boxes in shaping the SMOPI strength18, we used a convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture (see the subsection “ANNs: model architecture and training protocol” in the “Methods” section), an AI model from the ANNs’ family, which is well-suited for extracting spatial features from gridded data31. CNNs effectively represent sub-regional atmospheric structures and capture complex non-linear interactions missed by traditional physics-based models.As previously mentioned, one of the prerequisites for a climate model to project a plausible future is its ability to realistically represent the historical climate and its underlying physical mechanisms. However, it is well-documented that many CMIP6 models struggle to accurately reproduce the WAM rainfall32. Some models exhibit structural biases linked to their internal physics, while others show biases stemming from the chaotic nature of their internal variability. Furthermore, the multi-model EnsMean is often not physically representative of any single member due to the cancellation of individual structural errors. To overcome these issues, we used a model’s cross-domain generalization approach17,33 to build a physics-weighted ANNs-based ensemble: we train each ANN individually on the raw outputs of CMIP6 models. Subsequently, each trained ANN is forced with the same reference data, in this study, the SLP boxes from JRA-55, used as predictors. Finally, the WAM precipitation (JJAS) predicted by each ANN is compared against observed rainfall data to evaluate the fidelity of the model’s physics relative to JRA-55 (Fig. 1, Supplementary Fig. 2). JRA-55 is used as the reference because it represents the intraseasonal and interannual precipitation variability more accurately than ERA5. It also better captures the teleconnections related to the SMOPI18. Such a redistribution has important implications for flood risk, soil erosion, and water management in the WAM region39,40.DiscussionRefining models’ diversity in projections of WAM precipitation remains a major challenge for providing reliable climate services in the region. Despite CMIP6 models’ advances in complexity, they still show disparate results, alternating between significant drying and increased wetness3,4. Our results suggest that this spread is not limited to model resolution but is deeply linked to how models simulate large-scale atmospheric factors. By anchoring precipitation projections to the SMOPI SLP boxes, we move beyond simply comparing rainfall amounts to a process-oriented assessment of the physical mechanisms.The ability of ANNs to learn these relationships offers a considerable advantage over traditional ensemble means. While the ‘model democracy’ approach considers all simulations as equally plausible, our physics-guided weighted ANN recognizes that some models reproduce regional teleconnections much more realistically than others11. This is particularly evident when comparing the BEST and RESM model groups. We found that models with a more accurate representation of SMOPI dynamics tend to produce more constrained and physically consistent projections. Interestingly, a model can correlate well with observed precipitation for the wrong reasons, such as internal error compensation, if its underlying teleconnection schemes are unrealistic.In addition, the stability of the learned physical relationship between different members of the ensemble over time confirms the robustness of the deep learning architecture. By integrating historical and future climate states into the training process, ANNs can better account for potential non-stationarity in radiative forcing scenarios, such as the SSP5-8.5 scenario used in this study. Additionally, ANNs-based projections show clearer emerging signals of precipitation change, suggesting that conditioning on physically realistic circulation drivers isolates robust climate change responses from model noise. This helps bridge the gap between historical performance and future reliability, a common limitation of climate model weighting.A common concern when using ANNs trained with mean squared error (MSE) objectives under climate distributional shifts is the risk of “mode averaging” or artificial variance reduction, which can lead to ensemble responses featured by overconfidence and excessive smoothing. In the present study, however, the ANN optimization is driven by a Tweedie-based loss function combined with an amplitude-preserving constraint, rather than by a pure MSE objective alone. This hybrid formulation helps preserve the statistical distribution and intensity variability of precipitation fields while limiting excessive variance damping.However, when comparing the “BEST ANNs” and “BEST Raws”, it emerges that the ANN-based approach does not suffer from a collapse toward unrealistic mean solutions. Instead, the ANN ensemble preserves regional variability and physically interpretable spatial structures, which remain dynamically consistent with the behaviour of the underlying model. The reduction in inter-model spread, therefore, stems from the explicit synergy of our two-step approach rather than from statistical over-smoothing induced by the ANN optimization itself. First, the individual ANNs act as non-linear operators that filter out local model-specific parameterization biases, thereby reconstructing a physically cleaner and more coherent response within the ensemble. Second, the performance-based weighting scheme applies a complementary observational constraint by softly reducing the influence of dynamically inconsistent behaviours. Because our weighting approach uses a conservative, soft-constraint setup that avoids completely discarding models to prevent overconfidence (Supplementary Fig. 10), it does not act as an aggressive statistical filter. Instead, it works in conjunction with the ANN physical reconstructions to narrow the inter-model dispersion while fully preserving the forced response and internal variability inherent to each individual climate model.Although the present ANN architecture improves the dynamical coherence of precipitation projections across models, it does not fully eliminate structural climate-model uncertainty. Because the ANN learns relationships embedded within CMIP6 simulations, residual biases inherited from the driving models may still remain. Future work should therefore investigate more rigorous out-of-sample validation strategies, including perfect-model experiments and multi-model leave-one-out techniques and multi-member ANN training approaches to further isolate externally forced signals from the internal variability of specific realizations.The systematic shift toward higher rainfall intensities observed in our physics-guided weighted projections fits within the broader understanding of the intensification of the hydrological cycle in West Africa37,38. Even when mean rainfall changes remain moderate, the log-scale diagnostic of the distribution tails shows a shift toward higher thresholds, suggesting a robust increase in the frequency and intensity of heavy rainfall events under a warming climate. In a region where food security and water management are closely tied to monsoon variability, these observations, while constrained, provide a stronger scientific basis for adaptation strategies. This work also unveils that combining physical indices such as SMOPI and deep learning allows us to eliminate less reliable signals and reveal the future pathway where climate models achieve the highest physical consensus. This two-step paradigm can be easily transposed to other monsoonal systems or climate variables globally.MethodsModels and reanalysis datasetsDaily simulations of sea-level pressure (SLP) and precipitation from 11 CMIP6 models (see Supplementary Table 1), including the historical and Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP)-585 scenarios, are utilized in this work. On the one hand, using a daily time step ensures that the high-frequency variability footprint of some related monsoon processes, such as the African easterly waves, a major driver of the monsoon convective system41,42, is captured. On the other hand, it provides the ANN with a sufficiently large statistical sample for robust convergence, thus avoiding the smoothing of key physical processes when averaged monthly or yearly. By using the SSP585 scenario, we ensure that the climate change signal is sufficiently maximized to be distinguishable from natural variability. In doing so, we assess the ability of our method to constrain the most divergent future pathways and reduce the inter-model spread in a context of extreme radiative forcing.Models are selected so that each of them must be available on at least two realizations (member 1 and member 2), and the required variables, namely SLP and precipitation, must be available for each of the realizations. To ensure the robustness of results and avoid overfitting due to internal climate variability, we adopted a cross-validation strategy. For each of the 11 CMIP6 models, the CNN architecture was trained using member 1. Predictive performance and future projections (up to 2100) were then evaluated using an independent implementation, i.e., member 2. This procedure ensures that the deep learning model identifies stable physical teleconnections between sea-level pressure and precipitation, which are consistent for different initial conditions within the same CMIP6 model. Notably, although the two members have different internal variability, they share a common physics so that there are no physical inconsistencies when applying the model inter-member transfer learning17,33.ANN models are informed by climate models’ physics via teleconnections between the SLP boxes of the SMOPI system and the WAM precipitation. The observed teleconnections are extracted from the Japanese 55-year reanalysis (JRA-5519), which has a spatial resolution of 1.25° × 1.25°. Alongside JRA-55, we added the fifth-generation atmospheric reanalysis from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF) (ERA543) to account for uncertainties in the reference datasets. Although ERA5 has a higher resolution than JRA-55, the latter is used as the reference dataset throughout the study. Indeed, relative to ERA5, JRA-55 better represents the interannual variability of WAM precipitation as well as its teleconnection with the SMOPI18. To ensure that generated predictions not only reflect the physics-based reanalyses but also are grounded in observed reality, two gridded observational products were included in analyses: the Climatic Research Unit gridded Time Series (CRU TS4.0844) observational dataset, with a resolution of 0.5° × 0.5°, and the Global Precipitation Climatology Center version 8 (GPCC) with a 0.5° × 0.5° grid spacing45. These two observational datasets were chosen not only for their reliability46 but also because of their availability from the beginning of the 20th century to the present day. As the production of the JRA-55 reanalysis only began in 1958, the historical data were selected from 1958 to 2014. The projections span from 2015 to 2100. All datasets were regridded to a common 1.25° × 1.25° resolution, matching the JRA-55 reference grid using the conservative remapping to minimize alterations in spatial gradients.Sahel monsoon ocean-pressure index (SMOPI)In this study, we aim to train ANN models to predict precipitation at a climatological scale. This requires transferring the physical processes that drive rainfall into ANNs. Precipitation in a region results from complex mechanisms that act at different scales, from local to global, and from hourly to multidecadal. Therefore, choosing the right predictor is essential for the ANNs to produce realistic results. The SMOPI is an ideal predictor for this task. Indeed, this index captures both large-scale, regional, and local features and thus global climate drivers of the Sahel monsoon system18. It is based on SLP in five specific regions of the tropical oceanic and continental basins. These regions were selected because their pressure variations are closely linearly and non-linearly linked to Sahel rainfall. The SMOPI is calculated as a weighted linear combination of the weighted box-averaged SLP values:$${{{SMOPI}}}=\frac{1}{4}({\beta }_{1}{{{{SLP}}}}_{1}+{\beta }_{2}{{{{SLP}}}}_{2}+{\beta }_{3}{{{{SLP}}}}_{3}+{\beta }_{4}{{{{SLP}}}}_{4})-{\beta }_{5}{{{{SLP}}}}_{5}$$
                    (1)
                where \({\beta }_{1},...,{\beta }_{5}\) are the weights for each SLP region, respectively, representing the size and shape of their grids and approximating their concrete contribution to the entire SMOPI strength. To apply the SMOPI formula, the SLP anomaly within each of the five SMOPI boxes (\({\beta }_{k}{{{{SLP}}}}_{k}\)) is calculated as a spatial area-weighted mean to account for the convergence of meridians toward the poles. Specifically, the weighted mean for a given box is defined as$${\beta }_{k}{{{{SLP}}}}_{k}\left(t\right)=\frac{{\varSigma }_{i,j}{{{SLP}}}\left(i,j,t\right){{{\rm{\cdot }}}} cos ({\phi }_{i})}{{\varSigma }_{i,j} cos ({\phi }_{i})}{{with}}\,k=({1},\,{2},\,{3},\,{4},\,{5})$$
                    (2)
                where \({{{SLP}}}\left(i,j,t\right)\) denotes the SLP at longitude grid point i, latitude grid point j, and at the time step t, and \({\phi }_{i}\) represents the latitude. This formulation ensures that the weighting factor depends exclusively on latitudinal geography and remains completely independent of the atmospheric variable being averaged.The intensity of SMOPI (\({I}_{{{\rm {SMOPI}}}}\)) is defined as the standardized anomaly of SMOPI, such that:$${I}_{SMOPI}=\frac{{{\rm {SMOPI}}}-\overline{{{\rm {SMOPI}}}}}{{\sigma }_{{{\rm {SMOPI}}}}}$$
                    (3)
                where \(\overline{SMOPI}\) is the long-term mean of SMOPI, and \({\sigma }_{{SMOPI}}\) represents its standard deviation. As defined, the SMOPI can be used across different scales, from subseasonal to multidecadal. Positive SMOPI intensity values correspond to stronger monsoon conditions, while negative values indicate weaker conditions. Although the SMOPI was originally developed for the Sahel region18, the large-scale pressure anomalies it captures are closely linked to the monsoon dynamics governing West Africa as a whole. Therefore, this study employs the SMOPI as a robust predictor for monsoon precipitation across the entire West African domain.ANNs: model architecture and training protocolANNs are used to learn the relationship between large-scale pressure patterns and WAM precipitation. In the same domain, CMIP6 models do not perform similarly compared to observations. Some are closer to observations than others, generally in association with the realism of their internal physics. However, the performance of a model also depends on its internal variability47. Even if a model has very realistic physics, it may not perfectly match observations due to its own chaotic fluctuations. This is why we trained each ANN on an individual model. This way, we avoid inconsistencies between the internal physical mechanisms of different models and ensure that each ANN learns the specific climate signals of its corresponding model. The ANN inputs consist of SLP fields extracted from the five SMOPI boxes (Supplementary Fig. 1), while the output corresponds to JJAS precipitation over West Africa on a regular latlon grid.The ANN is implemented as a convolutional neural network (CNN) with multiple parallel input branches (Conv-Branch 1–5; Fig. 6a). Each SMOPI SLP box is processed independently through a dedicated convolutional branch composed of two convolutional layers followed by adaptive average pooling. This design helps the network to extract spatial features specific to each pressure region. The outputs of all branches are subsequently concatenated and passed through a series of completely connected dense layers, which learn the combined influence of the different SLP regions. The final layer reshapes the output into a two-dimensional latlon precipitation field. A softplus activation function is applied to ensure non-negative precipitation values.Fig. 6: Architecture of the multi-branch convolutional neural network (CNN), training protocol to predict the WAM precipitation and workflow.Full size imagea The schematic illustrates the complete workflow from large-scale atmospheric predictors to precipitation fields. Input layers are large-scale sea-level pressure (SLP) fields, extracted from the five SMOPI predictor boxes. Feature extraction of each SLP box is processed independently through a dedicated parallel convolutional branch (Conv-Branch 1–5). Each branch consists of two convolutional layers with 32 filters each, integrated with dropout regularization (rate = 0.2) to limit overfitting. Spatial features are further downsampled using adaptive average pooling layers to capture the dominant regional variability signals. The extracted feature maps from all five branches are concatenated into a single feature vector, which is passed through a series of dense (fully connected) layers with 128, 96 and 48 units, respectively. A final dense layer followed by a reshape operation generates the two-dimensional lat-lon precipitation field. A softplus activation function is applied to the output to ensure physically consistent, non-negative precipitation values. The ANN training employs a hybrid Tweedie-amplitude loss function (with p = 1.5) to handle the zero-inflated nature of rainfall while maintaining monsoon intensity and phase. Optimization is conducted using the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 10-3 over 500 epochs. To ensure robustness and physical consistency, an ensemble of 50 realizations is trained for each individual CMIP6 model, with the final prediction representing the ensemble mean. b A flowchart tracking the progression from raw datasets to the extraction of the five SLP predictor boxes for SMOPI, through model-specific CNN training and cross-member validation, to the final process-oriented weighting and generation of future WAM precipitation projections under the high-emission SSP5-8.5 scenario.The ANNs are trained using supervised learning. We used a hybrid loss function, the Tweedie-amplitude loss. It handles the specific nature of West African rainfall. The Tweedie component48 is ideal for precipitation because it effectively models data with many zeros and a continuous positive distribution. We improved the model’s ability to capture extreme events by adding an amplitude constraint. This constraint uses a normalized mean squared error (MSE) to ensure the model properly simulates the intensity and phase of the monsoon49. By doing so, we constrain the model to focus on both the temporal variability and the intensity of precipitation, while limiting excessive smoothing or amplitude bias. Model parameters are optimized using the Adam optimizer. To improve robustness and reduce sensitivity to random initialization, an ensemble of 50 ANN realizations is trained for each model. The final ANN prediction is obtained as the ensemble mean. Training is performed using mixed-precision computation on graphics processing units (GPUs).We conducted two rounds of training: (1) the first round consisted of assessing the physical realism of each CMIP6 model using member 1. Here, the ANNs are trained over the historical period using CMIP6 simulations. After training, ANNs are forced with SLP fields from the JRA-55 reanalysis. This configuration enables the evaluation of the physical realism of each CMIP6 model by comparing the ANN-predicted precipitation with the reference JRA-55 precipitation. Model performance is quantified using grid-point temporal correlation analysis rather than spatial pattern correlations. This is because, instead of assessing only the similarities in the mean spatial structures, the grid-point temporal correlation, after aggregating into a single score using a Fisher z-transformation50, also allows evaluating consistencies of local temporal variabilities and, therefore, provides a more process-oriented assessment of model realism. The Fisher z-transformation is then spatially area-averaged and back-transformed, following the equation:$${r}_{mean}=tanh \left(\frac{1}{N}{\sum }_{i=1}^{N}{arctanh}({r}_{i})\right)$$
                    (4)
                where \({r}_{i}\) is the significant (p < 0.05) temporal correlation at grid point i, and N is the total number of significant grid-points. We compared correlations between, on the one hand, raw CMIP6 model rainfall data against JRA-55 rainfall data, and on the other hand, predicted rainfall data when each CNN is forced by JRA-55 against the same JRA-55 data. The ANNs’ fidelity to distribute WAM precipitation is also assessed by comparing the cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) of raw CMIP6 models and ANN-forced outputs against observational datasets. The performance is quantified using the Wasserstein distance (WD51), also known as the Earth mover’s distance. WD estimates the distance between two probability distributions. A lower WD value suggests that the model distribution is closer to the observations. The WD between the model distribution (M) and the observation distribution (O) is calculated as follows:$${WD} \left({{M,O}}\right)=\int \left|{F}_{M} \left(x\right)-{F}_{{{{\rm{O}}}}}\left(x\right)\right|{d}{x}$$
                    (5)
                where \({F}_{{\rm {M}}}\) and \({F}_{{{{\rm{O}}}}}\) are the CDFs of the modelled and observed WAM JJAS precipitation, respectively. (2) In a second experiment, we applied the model inter-member transfer learning, where ANNs are trained using CMIP6 member 1 data over the full period from 1958 to 2100, including historical and future projections. Each trained ANN is then applied to member 2 of the same model over the same period. This strategy evaluates the ANN’s ability to generalize across ensemble members while preserving the model-specific forced response and internal variability. However, this approach should not be interpreted as a completely independent observational validation of future climate projections, since both training and evaluation remain within the same underlying model structure. Rather, the objective is to assess the dynamical consistency and robustness of the learned SLP-precipitation relationships across different realizations of the same climate model. A schematic of the flowchart of the experimental setup, showing inputs, outputs, and validation modalities for each step of the pipeline, is summarized in Fig. 6b.All ANN models were trained using a fixed and common set of hyperparameters for all experiments and CMIP6 models. For all rounds of the training process, we used the TensorFlow package, applied a learning rate of 10−3, and a dropout regularization of 0.2 in all convolutional branches to reduce overfitting. The batch size corresponds to the full training set, as the predictors and targets are provided as complete temporal samples. Each convolutional layer uses 32 filters, and the same architecture was used across all realizations, each realization running over 500 epochs. We implemented early stopping based on the validation loss, using a patience of 15 epochs and a minimum improvement threshold of 10−4, with the option of restoring the best weights at the end of the training. The loss function based on the Tweedie deviance utilized a fixed power parameter of p = 1.5 (corresponding to the Poisson–Gamma distribution49), combined with a normalized amplitude constraint weighted by α = 0.1. This is because precipitation is a non-negative, highly skewed variable characterized by a mixture of zero and positive values. It can therefore be approximated by a Poisson–Gamma (Tweedie) distribution, which accounts for both dry events and continuous rainfall intensities. No hyperparameter tuning was performed, ensuring that differences in performance arise from the predictors and the learning task rather than from model optimization.The pseudo-observation approachTo assess the physical consistency and robustness of ANNs, the raw outputs of the CMIP6 models are treated as surrogate observations, enabling an objective evaluation of ANN predictions for both historical and future periods. The ANN predictions for WAM precipitation are generated from CMIP6-derived predictors over the same time windows as the corresponding raw CMIP6 precipitation. Evaluation is done separately for historical and future periods to guarantee the temporal consistency between the ANN outputs and the CMIP6 fields. This approach helps us to verify whether the spatial and temporal patterns learned by the ANN remain consistent with the dynamics of the underlying climate model. The similarity of patterns between ANN predictions and raw CMIP6 fields is quantified using the above-mentioned Fisher’s z-transformation. The pseudo-observation method is intended as an internal dynamical consistency test to evaluate whether the ANN preserves the large-scale SLP–precipitation relationships embedded within each CMIP6 model. High agreement between ANN predictions and raw CMIP6 precipitation fields, therefore, indicates that the ANN successfully reproduces the model-specific teleconnection structures and associated forced response across ensemble members. However, this agreement alone does not guarantee that these relationships are fully representative of the real climate system, since structural biases inherited from the driving climate models may still remain. In this study, the observational constraint is introduced through the historical evaluation and weighting approach in association with the physics-guided ANN reconstruction (see the section “ANNs’ ensemble-mean construction approach” section). Models whose ANN-derived teleconnection structures more closely reproduce the JRA-55 dynamical relationships predict more realistic precipitation and receive larger weights in the final ensemble.ANNs’ ensemble-mean construction approachClimate model projections are commonly analysed using a simple ensemble mean, where all models are weighted equally7. This ‘model democracy’ approach reduces random errors, but it assumes that all models are equally realistic. While other studies use weighted ensembles, they often calculate weights using raw data10,52. This preserves internal model noise, which can lead to spurious results. In this study, we use ANNs to create a physics-weighted multi-ANN ensemble mean. Here, weights reflect how closely each CMIP6-driven ANN matches the JRA-55 reanalysis, which we use as the reference for realistic atmospheric dynamics. The weight assigned to the i-th ANN is defined as the likelihood that observations originate from that ANN. In practice, the likelihood of the ith CMIP6-driven ANN is expressed as a generalized distance-based Softmax function53 controlled by a temperature (or sharpness) scaling parameter τ defined as$${w}_{i}=\frac{exp (-\frac{{d}_{i}^{2}}{2\tau })}{{\sum }_{j=1}^{N}exp (-\frac{{d}_{j}^{2}}{2\tau })}$$
                    (6)
                where di is the normalized distance between the CMIP6-driven ANN output and the observation, expressed as$${d}_{i}=\sqrt{2\left(1-{r}_{i}\right)}$$
                    (7)
                where \({r}_{i}\) is the spatially averaged Fisher z-transformed and back-transformed temporal correlation of grid points between the ith CMIP6-driven ANN output and the observation. Under the default conservative setup (τ = 1), substituting the distance metric (Eq. 7) into the Softmax likelihood formulation (Eq. (6)) algebraically simplifies to a function directly scaling with the correlation coefficient:$${w}_{i}=\frac{exp ({r}_{i}-1)}{{\sum }_{j=1}^{N}exp ({r}_{j}-1)}$$
                    (8)
                where N is the total number of ANNs in the ensemble. This formulation ensures that all weights are positive and sum to one, while emphasizing models that better reproduce the reference teleconnection physics (i.e., higher correlations lead to larger weights).To evaluate the mathematical robustness of this filter and prevent risks of overconfident climate projections, a comprehensive ablation and sensitivity study exploring alternative weighting formulations using linear54 (i.e., \({w}_{i}=\frac{\max \left({r}_{i},0\right)}{{\sum }_{j=1}^{N}\max ({r}_{j},0)}\)) and quadratic55 (\({w}_{i}=\frac{{r}_{i}^{2}}{{\sum }_{j=1}^{N}{r}_{j}^{2}}\)) and varying degrees of sharpness (τ = 1, 0.2, 0.05) was performed (see Supplementary Fig. 10). This analysis demonstrates that the default setup used (Eq. (8)) acts as a safe, conservative, soft constraint that retains ensemble diversity. We deliberately focus on this soft-constraint approach because it avoids overconfidence by accounting for the shared signal of the majority of the models, rather than aggressively favouring a single outlier. This approach fosters the combined effects of the weighting scheme and the physics-guided ANN reconstruction, both of which contribute to the overall reduction in inter-model spread. The physics-weighted multi-ANN ensemble mean is calculated as$${P}_{ANN}={\sum }_{n=1}^{N}\omega (n)P(n)$$

The spread is defined as the inter-model dispersion of the ensemble and is evaluated consistently for both approaches. First, JJAS precipitation changes are calculated by subtracting the 30-year (1985–2014) historical climatology from the yearly mean JJAS value. The inter-model range at each time step is defined as the difference between the maximum and minimum values within the ensemble after smoothing each raw model or ANNs-based projection over 30 years. The spread over the full projection period is estimated using an integrated metric. This metric is defined as the time-integrated inter-model range, calculated as the area between the maximum and minimum curves of the ensemble. The relative spread reduction (ΔU) achieved by the ANNs-based approach is then expressed as a percentage decrease of this area compared to the raw CMIP6 ensemble:$$\% \Delta U=\frac{{A}_{RAW}-{A}_{ANN}}{{A}_{RAW}} \times 100$$
                    (10)
                $${{\rm {With}} \,A}=\int \left(max - min \right){d}t$$
                    (11)
                where \({A}_{{{\rm {RAW}}}}\) and \({A}_{{{\rm {ANN}}}}\) represent the integrated inter-model ranges for the raw and ANNs-based projections, respectively.

Quantifying UK coastal flood exposure under future sea-level rise to 2300
                    M. D. Palmer 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0001-7422-198X1,2, J. Savage 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0003-4807-09163, P. D. Bates 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0001-9192-99633,4 & …J. Neal 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0001-5793-95943,4 Show authors

Nature Communications

volume 17,  Article number: 5882 (2026) Cite this article

Subjects
        
            Climate-change impactsProjection and prediction

AbstractThe latest Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change assessment report highlighted the potential for more than 15 m of global sea-level rise by 2300. In this study, we explore the implications for UK coastal flood exposure by combining national-scale flood modelling with physically-based storylines of UK sea-level rise. By 2100 all storylines show broadly similar results with at least an additional 0.5 million people exposed to the 1-in-200 year undefended flood extent, which represents a 25% increase compared to present day. Under the most pessimistic storyline by 2300 involving significant ice-sheet instability, an additional 13 million people could be exposed to the 1-in-200 year undefended flood event. This would imply the potential need for large-scale movement of populations and settlements away from the coast in the coming centuries. Given current global emissions pledges, exposure increases by 1.7 million people by 2300, however up to 1 million could be avoided if Paris Agreement targets for greenhouse gas emissions are met.

                        IntroductionSea-level rise poses an existential threat to coastal communities and ecosystems around the world1. Global mean sea level (GMSL) increased by about 20 ± 5 cm over the period 1901–2018, with a marked acceleration since the 1960s2. Since the 1990s, the net contribution from ice sheet mass loss has increased by a factor of four, and these huge ice reservoirs remain the primary threat for sea-level rise in the coming centuries2,3. The UK is an ideal natural laboratory in which to examine the implications of these possible changes, given the large coastal flood exposure and complex interaction of different sea-level rise drivers for this location. While the observed increase in UK-average sea level of 18 ± 3 cm over the period 1900–2022 is in good agreement with GMSL, there are important spatial variations in the UK rate of rise associated with Glacial Isostatic Adjustment (GIA)4. In England alone, a recent study suggests that there are currently 544,000 residential and 72,000 non-residential properties in the coastal floodplain, an amount equivalent to 2.5% of the total national building stock5. Even when flood defences are accounted for, approximately 10% of these coastal floodplain properties are exposed to events with a return period of less than 75 years. This could increase substantially under sea-level rise scenarios, and this has the potential to significantly reshape the geography of the UK coast.Previous studies have highlighted the consequences of climate policy decisions in the next few decades for determining sea-level rise outcomes for centuries and millennia to come, illustrating the importance of early emissions reductions and raising questions about intergenerational justice2,6,7. The IPCC Sixth Assessment Report of Working Group I (IPCC AR6) stated that by 2300, GMSL will increase by 0.3–3.1 m under low emissions (SSP1-2.6) and 1.7–6.8 m under high emissions (SSP5-8.5), increasing up to 16 m for SSP5-8.5 if uncertain ice sheet instability processes are included2,8. This wide range of potential outcomes has motivated recent studies to pursue a storyline approach, where a small number of singular and physically-consistent trajectories of future sea-level rise are generated that span the overall uncertainty space9,10.The current national UK sea-level projections do not include the possibility of accelerated sea-level rise associated with uncertain ice sheet instability processes11,12, and current UK guidance on a “credible maximum (H++)” sea-level rise by 2100 is 1.9 m13 (www.gov.uk/guidance/flood-and-coastal-risk-projects-schemes-and-strategies-climate-change-allowances), yet sea-level rise in London could reach 5 m by 2150 and more than 15 m by 2300, based on outcomes highlighted in IPCC AR62,8,10. Therefore, the goal of the present study is to provide a comprehensive analysis of the implications of IPCC AR6 sea-level projections out to 2300 for UK coastal flooding and coastline retreat. While coastal flood hazard is also subject to changes in storm surges, waves and tides, these are secondary factors compared to the century timescale threat from sea-level rise14 and therefore neglected from this study.Current estimates of coastal flooding produced by the UK Government and others often use so-called ‘bathtub models’ to predict inundation. These take the extreme water level at the coast and project it inland, with the assumption that any land below this elevation is inundated even if, in practice, this is physically impossible due to dynamical effects or a lack of hydraulic connectivity15. Recent high-profile global studies looking at sea-level rise impacts16,17,18,19,20 also invariably use bathtub methods. Instead, to realistically model coastal inundation, a numerical hydrodynamic model is needed that properly represents the physics and time dynamics of shallow water flow. Such models have previously only existed for individual coastal segments or river reaches, but recently the availability of better data, new numerical schemes and High Performance Computing has allowed hydrodynamic approaches to be applied to simulate flooding at national to global scales21,22,23,24.Our analysis is based on model simulations without flood defences for several reasons. Firstly, it allows us to identify: (i) new populations that could become exposed to flooding in the absence or failure of flood defences; (ii) infrastructure or land that could become exposed to floods, which could help inform decisions on whether areas require future investment in flood protection infrastructure; and (iii) locations that could be repurposed for relocated communities to inhabit. Secondly, there are no datasets that project flood defence standards out to 2300, and the level of investment in defences would also likely vary depending on the climate scenario followed. Lastly, if we assume defences remain at their current standards of protection, we would learn very little about changing flood risk except in undefended and rural areas. Therefore, we feel that the undefended scenario provides a more complete picture of potential exposure to floods both in the present day and the future. We work with the present day population as a baseline because currently available UK future projections25 are: (i) ‘blind’ to flood risk and therefore allow expansion of population into areas which, in reality, would never be developed; (ii) only available at 1 km resolution which is insufficiently granular for a localised problem such as flooding; and (iii) only exist out to 2100 as beyond this uncertainties are simply too great. It should be noted, however, that the population is not static and future work should incorporate these effects once appropriate projections become available.This study uses a recently published set of physically-consistent storylines of UK future sea-level rise that span the full range of potential outcomes to 2300 across the low emissions (SSP1-2.6) and high emissions (SSP5-8.5) scenarios, including ice sheet collapse, highlighted in IPCC AR63,10. While we acknowledge that high emissions futures are considered unlikely26, the sea-level rise outcomes associated with simulations run under these scenarios are important for a more complete understanding of the total risk landscape and for risk-averse decision contexts27,28. These are then used within the 1 arcsecond (25 m) spatial resolution whole UK hydrodynamic model of Bates et al.23 to simulate the area at risk of flooding during storm events, given the different sea-level rise scenarios. This whole UK model is unique in being able to simulate coastal inundation from any plausible boundary conditions with fine spatial resolution and high skill (see “Methods” for more details). The storylines are based on the same underlying projection machinery as the UKCP18 sea-level projections11,29 and are therefore consistent with that information, which forms the basis of current UK planning. The results presented here are based on the five storylines of future UK sea-level rise from Palmer et al.10 with a focus on two for the flood modelling results. Storyline B is used as a baseline scenario and is broadly consistent with current international greenhouse gas emissions pledges. Storyline H2 is used as a “reasonable worst case scenario” under high greenhouse gas emissions and includes representation of poorly-understood ice sheet instability processes (see Supplementary Note S1). While both H1 and H2 could be used as a reasonable worst-case scenario, we focus on H2 because it corresponds to the Low-Likelihood High-Impact storyline that was given prominence in the IPCC AR6 Summary for Policymakers and more completely illustrates the risk that could be avoided through effective global action to reduce greenhouse gas emissions28. In this work, we characterise the coastal flood impacts at 2100, 2200 and 2300 associated with the sea-level rise storylines given the present-day population for the UK as a whole and for the UK capital cities of Belfast, Cardiff, London and Edinburgh. Simulations are based on the 1-in-200-year return period extreme coastal water level event from the UK Environment Agency coastal flood boundary condition dataset (see “Methods”) since this is the typical design standard of UK coastal flood defences in urban areas.ResultsSea-level rise storylines and spatial patternsThe storylines used in this study represent a broad range of outcomes for global mean sea-level (GMSL) rise from less than 1 m to more than 16 m by 2300 (Fig. 1a, Table 1). Story A, B and C show a near-linear rise of GMSL and span the overall range of the likely projections from IPCC AR6 across the SSP1-2.6 and SSP5-8.5 emissions scenarios. Storylines H1 and H2 show a marked acceleration in GMSL rise between 2050 and 2150 associated with ice sheet instabilities and correspondingly much larger rates and magnitudes of sea-level rise over the coming centuries. The model simulations underlying the storylines are based on assumptions of reducing greenhouse gas emissions30 from the 2020 s (Storyline A), around 2040 (Storyline B) or from 2150 (Storylines C, H1, H2) with a subsequent decrease in the rate of GMSL rise thereafter (Fig. 1a). The local expression of relative sea-level rise across the UK and Ireland in the coming centuries shows large spatial variations from the global average that results from three main factors: (i) the ongoing effects on local sea level from GIA31; and the spatial patterns of change associated with the (ii) Greenland and (iii) Antarctic ice sheets10,32. Spatial patterns of sea-level rise at 2300 for Storylines A and B (Fig. 1b, c) are dominated by GIA with the characteristic pattern of vertical land uplift in the north and land subsidence in the south. For example, this effect substantially reduces the 2300 sea-level rise values for Belfast and Edinburgh to about 0.1–0.2 m, compared to 0.6–0.7 m for Cardiff and London in Storyline A. Storyline C also exhibits a strong imprint of GIA in the spatial pattern of sea-level rise (Fig. 1d) with values across the UK ranging from 3.5–4.5 m. The influence of spatial patterns associated with the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets is more evident for Storylines H1 and H2 (Fig. 1e, f), with values at 2300 ranging from about 8.5–9.5 m and 16.5–17.5 m, respectively.Fig. 1: sea-level rise storylines and 2300 spatial patterns.Full size imagea Time series of global mean sea-level (GMSL) rise for the five storylines presented in Palmer et al.10 as indicated in the figure legend. The grey-shaded region shows the overall IPCC AR6 likely range (i.e., the central two-thirds probability distribution) across the SSP1-2.6 and SSP5-8.5 greenhouse gas emissions scenarios to 2150. The grey dotted line shows the IPCC AR6 low-likelihood high-impact storyline presented in the Working Group I Summary for Policymakers3. b–f The spatial pattern of relative sea-level rise at 2300 associated with each storyline. All sea-level rise projections are expressed relative to the 1986–2005 average.Table 1 Summary of sea-level rise storylines used in this studyFull size tableThe flood mapping and impacts analysis presented here focuses on Storyline B as a baseline scenario (in the absence of further global greenhouse gas emissions pledges) and Storyline H2 as a “reasonable worst case” scenario for informing future coastal adaptation planning. We choose Storyline B as our baseline rather than Storyline A because the latter could be considered an overly optimistic basis for adaptation planning, given that it goes beyond current emissions pledges and assumes a weak sea-level response to future warming (Table 1). While we cannot give a robust likelihood for Storyline H2, we assess that it is broadly consistent with the UK National Risk Register definition of “reasonable worst case” of being “a challenging manifestation of the scenario after highly implausible scenarios are excluded” and note that IPCC AR6 states that this outcome cannot be ruled out under high emissions3. For a discussion of what constitutes “reasonable” in this context, please see Supplementary Note S1. GMSL rise at 2100 reaches approximately 0.6 m for Storyline B and 1.5 m for Storyline H2 (Fig. 1a), with large geographical variations across the UK and Ireland (Supplementary Fig. 1).Impacts of sea-level rise on UK coastal flood hazardAt a national scale, the changes in undefended inundation from a 1-in-200 year storm surge event (i.e., the basis of flood defence standards in the UK) shows modest changes with future sea-level rise at 2100 (Fig. 2A). The greatest areas of increased inundation are found for The Wash and the Humber Estuary on the east coast of England with a 13% national increase in total flood extent for Storyline B and 41% increase for Storyline H2 (Fig. 2A, Supplementary Table 3). To illustrate the local impacts of sea-level rise, we also present detailed mapping for the UK capital cities of Belfast (2B), Cardiff (2C), Edinburgh (2D) and London (2E), along with the present-day area at risk. For Storyline B by 2100, the additional areas of inundation are relatively modest. Given climate change and uncertainty tolerances within flood defence design33, it is likely that the real-world impacts of a ~ 0.5 m sea-level rise in areas protected by coastal flood defences would be limited. Nevertheless, many UK port facilities in southern England, which are necessarily outside of flood defences, will be impacted by a ~ 0.5 m rise in sea level due to the increase in extreme water levels during coastal surge events, and this may require additional protection measures to be adopted following port planning guidance and sector-specific climate change risk assessments34,35. For scenario H2 by 2100, the UK sea-level rise range of 1.2–1.5 m is more problematic, with large areas of west London, central Cardiff and infrastructure such as Belfast Airport within the zone inundated by the 1-in-200 year event. For H2, sea-level rise by 2100 is at the upper limit of what any present-day defences could plausibly protect against, so we can more definitively say these are areas that are not currently at risk but would be in the future.Fig. 2: Flood maps including sea-level rise to 2100.Full size imageA Flood inundation map for the UK based on the 1-in-200-year return period for the present day and with sea-level rise for Storylines B and H2 at 2100 in the absence of flood defences, as indicated in the figure legend. Panels B–E show local flood maps for Belfast, Cardiff, Edinburgh and London.By 2300, both Storyline B and Storyline H2 imply dramatic changes for the UK coastal flood hazard (Fig. 3A). The Storyline B local relative sea-level rise of about 1.2–1.8 m across the UK translates, in the absence of flood defences, to a 56% increase in the flood area of the 1-in-200-year storm surge event (Fig. 1c, Supplementary Table 3). For Storyline H2, the local sea-level rise at 2300 ranges from about 16.5–17.5 m with more than a 300% increase in flood area for the 1-in-200-year surge event (Fig. 1f, Supplementary Table 3). For this amount of sea-level rise, present-day flood defences are largely irrelevant. At a national scale, for H2, it is The Wash and the Humber Estuary that show the largest change in area of land exposed to coastal flood hazard. However, we can now also see evidence of substantive changes in other parts of the United Kingdom, including the Thames estuary, Eastern Norfolk, North Somerset, Gloucestershire, Liverpool and the northwest coast of England. As before, Fig. 3 shows the details of inundation changes for the UK capital cities. Under Storyline B by 2300, some major public institutions, such as the Welsh parliament building (the Senedd) in Cardiff, now lie within the 200-year flood zone, along with major UK infrastructure such as Glasgow airport, Teesside chemical works and the port of Dover. In Storyline H2, many UK critical infrastructure locations are affected by flooding, including the M25 motorway (especially around Heathrow airport) and the financial district of the City of London. Nationally significant heritage, such as St. Paul’s Cathedral in London, lies within the flood zone, and large areas of west and north London are impacted by water depths in excess of 1 m. Along the east coast, the upland area of the Lincolnshire Wolds becomes an island during extreme floods, and coastal flooding here can even propagate inland as far as major cities such as Cambridge and York, both of which see their entire central areas flooded to depths of 1 m or more. Although we have not attempted to model changes in coastlines, Storyline H2 at 2300 would see large areas of low-lying land below the nominal high tide line and therefore permanently inundated.Fig. 3: Flood maps including sea-level rise to 2300.Full size imageA Flood inundation map for the UK based on the 1-in-200-year return period for the present day and with sea-level rise for Storylines B and H2 at 2300 in the absence of flood defences, as indicated in the figure legend. Panels B–E show local flood maps for Belfast, Cardiff, Edinburgh and London.The inundation maps have been combined with present-day UK population data36 to estimate the potential change in the population exposed to the 1-in-200 year flood event for each of the five storylines at 2100, 2200 and 2300 (Fig. 4). At 2100, all five storylines yield a modest increase in population exposure relative to the present day, with results indicating a low sensitivity to emissions pathways on this time-horizon. This outcome relates to the committed sea-level rise inherent to all storylines that is associated with past greenhouse gas emissions and the slow response of the ocean and cryosphere to surface warming2 (Supplementary Fig. 1). By 2200 there are much greater differences across the storylines associated with the broader range of sea-level rise outcomes (Supplementary Fig. 2) and even reductions in population exposure in Northern Ireland and Scotland for Storylines A and B where ongoing vertical land uplift associated with GIA overcomes the climate-change-induced sea-level rise. At 2300, the differences across storylines are even more pronounced, with the percentage of population exposed to the 1-in-200-year coastal flood extent exceeding 20% for England, Scotland and Wales under the H2 storyline (compared to between 1–3% in the present day).Fig. 4: UK population exposure based on sea-level rise storylines.Full size imagePopulation exposure for a England b Scotland c Wales d Northern Ireland at 2100, 2200 and 2300 for all sea-level rise storylines presented in the text, based on a 1-in-200-year return period. A 0.3 m threshold has been used to characterise the flood area (Supplementary Table 1). Numbers for alternative thresholds are available in the Supplementary Information.Although defences have not been explicitly modelled, we can infer from the inundation modelling when these defences would be overtopped for the various scenarios modelled. This can help identify tipping points in the scenario-time horizon space where significant investment or adaptation may be required to limit exposure to coastal flood events. The inundation maps have been intersected with defence crest elevations from the Environment Agency Asset Information Management System (AIMS) dataset37 to assess the proportion of defences in England for which the modelled water surface elevation exceeds their height. Under Storyline B, in 2100, <1% of defences are modelled to have a maximum water level exceeding the defence height by 1 m or more. This increases to 27% by 2200 and 35% by 2300. Comparatively, under Storyline H2, in 2100, 10% of defences are modelled to have a maximum water level exceeding the defence height by 1 m or more, increasing to nearly 100% by 2200. Further information on this approach is provided in Supplementary Note S3 with a table of results presented in Supplementary Table 8.DiscussionCurrent UK national planning guidance for sea-level rise focuses on the coming century only and includes allowances that range from about 1.0 to 1.6 m over the period 2000 to 2125, depending on geographic location (https://www.gov.uk/guidance/flood-risk-assessments-climate-change-allowances). Where it is appropriate to use a “credible maximum scenario”, planners are advised to use the H + + sea-level rise allowance value of 1.9 m38, which represents a value for the end of the 21st century—no guidance is provided beyond this time-horizon. In addition, residual uncertainty allowances (typically a few 10 s of cm) are implemented when building flood defences in the UK, affording some extra margin of protection33. At 2100, this combination of climate scenarios and residual uncertainty allowances should therefore likely accommodate the values of sea-level rise for the UK across all storylines that have peak values of about 1.5 m (Supplementary Fig. 1). Under storyline B, the 2100 population exposed to flooding increases by 25%, which is slightly below the 27% increase in properties at risk by 2069 predicted by the most recent UK National Flood Risk Assessment39 (NaFRA2). Therefore, our exposure storylines are broadly consistent while being conservative with respect to UK government projections this century. The estimated changes in UK population exposure are similar to previous studies under similar climate scenarios and flood defence assumptions, with an increase of approximately 0.5 million for Storyline B and approximately 1 million for Storyline C by 210040. Under Storyline B it is unlikely that hard flood defence adaptation limits will be reached by 2100 (Supplementary Table 8). This is also the case for the majority of defences for Storyline H2, although significant levels of investment would be required to increase the height of defences over the coming century (Supplementary Table 8).Beyond 2100, the sea-level storylines diverge markedly with large differences in the associated flood impacts by 2300 (Figs. 1, 3). Storyline A clearly illustrates the huge potential for avoided sea-level rise through swift and substantive global greenhouse gas emissions reductions consistent with Paris Agreement targets, with exposure increasing by only 28%. Conversely, Storyline H2 illustrates the vast threat of sea-level rise for the UK if ice sheet instability processes are triggered with values that far exceed the current UK H++ credible maximum scenario of 1.9 m within a few decades of 2100 and a five-fold increase in population exposure by 2300 - vastly outside the range reported in NaFRA239. While the UKCP18 national projections included sea-level rise information to 2300, this did not include an update to H++ or any equivalent credible maximum scenario on this time-horizon.Our results show many instances of major UK infrastructure moving into flood risk areas as the sea level continues to rise beyond 2100. Increased exposure to coastal flooding is identified across all storylines. Under Storyline B, approximately half of England’s coastal flood defences would need investment over the subsequent 200 years to maintain defence standards, with a small number potentially being beyond hard adaptation limits (Supplementary Table 8). Under Storyline H2, >99% of flood defences could already be beyond hard adaptation limits by 2200 (Supplementary Table 8). The increased population exposure to the 1-in-200-year flood event under the H2 storyline from 3 million to almost 10 million between 2100 and 2200 implies widespread disruption to the economy and society, with challenges compounded by potentially reaching hard adaptation limits (Supplementary Table 8). This scenario would require high levels of investment for both new and existing flood defences, potential movement of communities away from coastlines, and put critical infrastructure and sites of national strategic importance at high risk of disruption.It is therefore inevitable that a combination of additional or enhanced flood defences and managed retreat will be necessary to mitigate against post-2100 flood risk. Stakeholders who only consider changes over the coming century may have a false impression of the true risk landscape, given the potential for post-2100 acceleration of sea-level rise. Planning of long-lived infrastructure and future settlements must therefore be cognisant of the full range of possible outcomes for multi-century and longer-term committed sea-level rise to avoid costly future interventions.There is a clear need for continuous monitoring of sea-level rise with a particular emphasis on the ice sheets to understand the observed trajectory compared to expectations across a broad range of possible outcomes. This will allow as much time as possible to prepare for and react to extreme future sea-level rise should one of the more extreme scenarios be realised.The Thames Estuary 2100 project41 takes an adaptation pathways approach to managing future flood risk for London and planning of future adaptation measures throughout the estuary42,43. This approach triggers different adaptation options as various sea-level rise “milestones” are met. Combining our storylines with adaptive pathways approaches could form a powerful tool for reflexive learning and promoting robust adaptation decision-making42. However, previous work has suggested that the engineering limits to adaptation for the Thames Estuary would be surpassed at approximately 5 m of sea-level rise44, which raises major questions for the city of London under the H1 and H2 storylines presented here. For storylines H1 or H2, London reaches 5 m of sea-level rise at around 2150 or 2200 (Supplementary Table 4) with corresponding widespread flood implications across the UK. For multiple metres of sea-level rise, maintaining current coastlines would prove extremely challenging for most of the UK and would therefore likely necessitate large-scale movement of settlements, population and infrastructure away from the coast. Given the high associated costs and long planning time-horizons, it is vital to consider potential peak rates of future UK sea-level rise in adaptation planning processes in order to anticipate decision lead-times. Due to the country-wide connectivity of vital infrastructure, it is imperative that full cost-benefit analyses45,46 are undertaken at the national scale to fully understand the economic, political and societal impacts of coastal flooding under such extreme future sea-level rise scenarios. This type of assessment would require a set of plausible scenarios that include feedback between population dynamics and the evolving flood hazard under adaptation measures and future sea-level rise that extend into the coming centuries.Overall, our results clearly illustrate the need to consider multi-century time-horizons to fully appreciate the scale of the coastal adaptation challenge, given deep uncertainty in projections of future sea-level rise. The “reasonable worst case scenario” (storyline H2) implies a substantively altered UK coastline in the coming centuries, with a need for large-scale movement of population, settlements and infrastructure away from the coast. However, the results also indicate how the worst impacts of sea-level rise could be avoided in the coming centuries if effective global action can be taken to minimise future global greenhouse gas emissions. The key policy implications of our study are to inform near-term adaptation planning for the period out to 2100 and further motivate rapid and deep reductions in global greenhouse gas emissions to mitigate against the risk of accelerated sea-level rise from ice sheet instability processes in the centuries that follow.MethodsThe sea-level rise storylines used in this study are based on those presented in Palmer et al.10 and the reader is referred there for further details. The five storylines each represent a singular and continuous trajectory of future sea-level rise drawn from the underlying sets of large Monte Carlo simulations developed for UKCP18 under the RCP scenarios11,12. Each Monte Carlo set includes 450,000 simulations of the following contributions to GMSL rise: (i) global thermosteric sea-level rise; (ii) mass addition from Antarctica; (iii) mass addition from Greenland; (iv) mass addition from mountain glaciers; (v) changes in land water storage. The storylines are generated following a two-step process that is designed to provide close consistency with several literature-based estimates of GMSL rise and the underlying process-based contributions. First, the Monte Carlo set is filtered to retain only those members that match the target GMSL rise at the given time-horizon. Second, a single Monte Carlo member is selected that provides the best fit to the individual contributions (i)–(v). Storyline A is based on the RCP2.6 Monte Carlo simulations selected for consistency with the lower bound of the likely range (i.e. the 17th percentile) of the IPCC AR6 GMSL projections under SSP1-2.6 at 2150. Storyline B is based on the RCP4.5 Monte Carlo simulations and selected to be consistent with the central estimate (i.e. the 50th percentile) of the IPCC AR6 GMSL projections under SSP2-4.5 at 2150. Storyline C is based on the RCP8.5 Monte Carlo simulations and selected for consistency with the upper bound of the likely range (i.e. the 83rd percentile) of IPCC AR6 GMSL projections under SSP5-8.5 at 2150. Storylines H1 and H2 are both based on the RCP8.5 Monte Carlo simulations with the Antarctica component replaced by the DeConto et al.8 simulations that represent the marine ice cliff instability (MICI) mechanism for Antarctica47. H1 is selected for consistency with the high-end estimate of GMSL at 2300 developed by van de Wal et al.48. H2 is consistent with the IPCC AR6 SSP5-8.5 low confidence projections, 83rd percentile for GMSL rise at 23002. The GMSL storylines are localised for the UK by first combining timeseries of (ii)–(v) with the corresponding spatial patterns of Gravity, Rotation and solid-earth Deformation (GRD) to provide spatially complete information for across the domain of the UK and Ireland at 2100, 2200 and 2300. Secondly, timeseries of (i) are converted to a representative UK-average of the sterodynamic sea-level change using a spatially uniform regression coefficient based on the scenario-specific central estimates from UKCP18. These values are: 1.372 for SSP1-2.6/RCP2.6 (used for Storyline A); 1.390 for SSP2-4.5/RCP4.5 (used for Storyline B), and 1.465 for SSP5-8.5/RCP8.5 (used for Storyline C, H1, H2). All regression coefficients result in a time-invariant amplification of the global signal that is largest for the SSP5-8.5/RCP8.5 scenario. Further justification of this approach is presented in Supplementary Note S2. Finally, the spatial contribution to local sea-level change from Glacial Isostatic Adjustment (GIA) is added by assuming a linear rate of change and using the central estimate from the UKCP18 sea-level projections11,31.Projections of future flood hazard are based on the UK flood inundation model of Bates et al.23. This simulates floodplain flow by solving the local inertial form of the shallow water equations in two dimensions (2D) for a uniform grid using the numerical approach outlined in previous studies49,50. Channel flow is treated as a subgrid scale process solved in one dimension (1D) using the method of Neal et al.34 This allows river channels of any size to be represented, irrespective of the resolution of the overlying floodplain grid. The 2D model is run over the whole UK at 1 arcsecond resolution (20–25 m), with terrain elevations taken mostly from 10 cm vertical accuracy airborne laser altimetry (LiDAR) data, for which the coverage in the UK is approximately 70% and concentrated in lowland zones. The vertical datum is Ordnance Datum Newlyn in Great Britain and Ordnance Datum Belfast in Northern Ireland. Channel locations for the 1D component of the model are taken from UK Ordnance Survey data, with channel widths estimated based on hydraulic geometry relationships and channel bathymetry approximated using the gradually varied flow solver methodology of Neal et al.51 and channel friction of 0.04. We assume a bankfull return period of 1 in 2 years for natural alluvial channels. A fixed value of 0.06 is applied for the floodplain friction parameter in the model. Coastal boundary conditions for the model combine the storyline-based sea-level rise projections with the Environment Agency coastal flood boundary conditions dataset52 which defines the probability-magnitude of meteorologically-driven coastal extreme water levels above mean sea level around the UK. These extreme water heights were combined with the relevant storm surge profile for the stretch of coastline (as defined by the Environment Agency Design Surge Profile dataset), a time-varying profile based on historic tide gauge data and an estimate of wave setup (calculated using ERA5 reanalysis data53) to produce an extreme water height time series for the storm surge event that was simulated by the inundation model. Further details of the boundary condition and model discretisation can be found in Bates et al.23 who showed that this model could skilfully predict present-day flood areas and water depths when compared to UK Government official flood maps and post-event water depth observations.For this study, we re-simulated the inundation hydrodynamics of a 1-in-200-year extreme event (based on the central estimate) for UK coastal regions with peak water elevations increased to represent the impact of the five sea-level rise storylines 2100, 2200 and 2300. We simulated events with a return period of 1-in-200 years, as this is the current standard of protection for coastal flood defences in the UK and is typically presented in UK national flood risk maps. We use a version of our model without flood defences to provide a consistent baseline since we do not know the future trajectory of protection standards and because many of the storylines would exceed current design standards along most of the coastline outside London. Flood defences will mitigate the extent of flooding even when overwhelmed, however we chose to omit this second-order factor rather than include uncertain and spatially incomplete defence locations and heights from existing databases in the model. Readers should refer to Bates et al.20 and Environment Agency data for near-term hazard estimates that include existing flood defence standards. For each individual model, the maximum water level was defined and then converted into a water level time series through the event using standard tidal cycles. Our approach is supported by previous studies that have shown that mean sea level, tides and surge combine linearly, to a good approximation11,54. We acknowledge that the modelling approach neglects coastline and bathymetry changes associated with erosion and sedimentation processes, which could further modify extreme coastal water levels through associated tide and surge changes. These aspects are likely to be increasingly important under large degrees of future sea-level rise and warrant further research.Reporting summaryFurther information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

Article

Towards a theory for Earth’s albedo stability and hemispheric symmetry in the 21st Century
                    Daniel R. Feldman 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0003-3365-52331, Jake J. Gristey 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0003-1071-486X2,3,4, Maria Z. Hakuba 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0001-9895-40535, Doug Hellinger6 & …Samuel Kahn

Communications Earth & Environment

We are providing an unedited version of this manuscript to give early access to its
                            findings. Before final publication, the manuscript will undergo further editing. Please note
                            there may be errors present which affect the content, and all legal disclaimers apply.

Subjects
        
            Atmospheric scienceProjection and prediction

AbstractThe current scientific understanding of top-of-atmosphere globally-averaged albedo stability and hemispheric symmetry on interannual to centennial time-scales is largely phenomenological and diagnostic, leading to diverging albedo estimates over the 21st Century. We present a framework for hypothesis testing and theory development, complemented by observations, data methods, and models, to advance towards a theory for these phenomena. We present the theory’s necessary features needed and then explore two hypotheses and their observational tests: that albedo is (1) constrained by invariant Earth system properties, or (2) maintained by cloud buffering. We argue that there is a supporting role for artificial intelligence (AI) methods that express the non-linear processes that underlie these observed phenomena. Additionally, we show that the response to and relaxation from major perturbations like stratovolcanic eruptions may help to falsify hypotheses. Finally multi-model ensemble experiments and observations can support this multi-pronged approach to advance towards a working theory for albedo.
